The caption explains that the drum’s sound is as thunderous as lightning and far exceeds that of the Korean (or Chinese) taiko reputed in the region.]]
'''{{nihongo|Futon Daiko|ふとん太鼓}}''' are the large taiko platforms carried in festivals in the {{ill|Osaka Prefecture|en|Osaka Prefecture|qid=Q122723|lt=Osaka Prefecture}}, especially in the former provinces of {{ill|Kawachi Province|be|Каваты (правінцыя)|ca|Província de Kawachi|ckb|پارێزگای کاواچی|cs|Provincie Kawači|de|Provinz Kawachi|es|Provincia de Kawachi|fa|ولایت کاواچی|fr|Province de Kawachi|gl|Provincia de Kawachi|hak|Kawachi-koet|id|Provinsi Kawachi|it|Kawachi (provincia)|ja|河内国|ko|가와치국|lt|Kavačio žemė|nl|Kawachi (provincie)|pt|Província de Kawachi|ru|Кавати (провинция)|simple|Kawachi Province|sk|Kawači (provincia)|sr|Провинција Кавачи|tr|Kawachi (vilayet)|uk|Провінція Каваті|zh|河內國|zh_min_nan|Kawati-kok|zh_yue|河內國|qid=Q1047150|lt=Kawachi}} and {{ill|Izumi Province|ca|Província d'Izumi|ckb|پارێزگای ئیزومی|cs|Provincie Izumi|de|Provinz Izumi|es|Provincia de Izumi|fa|ولایت ایزومی|fr|Province d'Izumi|gl|Provincia de Izumi|hak|Izumi-koet|id|Provinsi Izumi|it|Izumi (provincia)|ja|和泉国|ko|이즈미국|lt|Idzumio žemė|nl|Izumi (provincie)|pt|Província de Izumi|ru|Идзуми (провинция)|simple|Izumi Province|sk|Izumi (provincia)|sr|Провинција Изуми|tr|Izumi (vilayet)|uk|Провінція Ідзумі|zh|和泉國|zh_min_nan|Izumi-kok|zh_yue|和泉國|qid=Q1047117|lt=Izumi}}, as well as in and around {{ill|Hyōgo Prefecture|en|Hyōgo Prefecture|qid=Q130290|lt=Hyōgo Prefecture}} (including the former provinces of {{ill|Harima Province|be|Харыма (правінцыя)|ca|Província de Harima|ceb|Harima (baranggay sa Hapon)|cs|Provincie Harima|de|Provinz Harima|es|Provincia de Harima|fa|ولایت هاریما|fr|Province de Harima|gl|Provincia de Harima|id|Provinsi Harima|it|Harima (provincia)|ja|播磨国|ko|하리마국|lt|Harimos žemė|nl|Harima (provincie)|pt|Província de Harima|ru|Харима (провинция)|simple|Harima Province|sk|Harima (provincia)|sr|Провинција Харима|tr|Harima (vilayet)|uk|Провінція Харіма|zh|播磨國|zh_min_nan|Harima-kok|qid=Q1047523|lt=Harima}} and {{ill|Awaji Province|en|Awaji Province|qid=Q1053717|lt=Awaji}}). They are a type of festival float ({{ill|Matsuri float|en|Matsuri float|qid=Q11470974|lt=Yamadashi}}) whose most striking feature is that a huge square futon (bedding) is stacked in an inverted-pyramid shape at what corresponds to its roof. They are also called futon danjiri, futon mikoshi, or simply futon floats.

== Format and Characteristics ==
*Common Features  
**Inside each futon taiko the central element is a taiko (drum) over which a group of youth, known as “{{ill|rider|ja|乗り子}}” (typically 4–8 in number), is seated. In some districts the riders are tied securely so that even in the midst of vigorous movement they do not fall off. The riders usually wear stage‐style heavy makeup ({{ill|thick ceremonial makeup|ja|厚化粧|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/thick ceremonial makeup|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11409220}}) and lavish costumes. They often use a club that is thick and short—resembling a shortened baseball bat—for striking.

*Osaka Type  
**This type is characterized by futons set at a relatively small angle and with carvings as the central decorative element. Carvings are also present on the {{ill|door panels|ja|土呂板}} and {{ill|Bridge|ja|欄干|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/railings|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 橋|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 橋|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q12280}}. Among these, some examples known as “{{ill|Yudai Taiko|ja|雄太鼓}}” are noted for their simplicity. A notable structural feature is the presence of a “{{ill|tagaya|ja|タガヤ}}”—a series of thin boards layered under the futon, arranged beneath a five-tiered section.

*Awaji Type  
**On {{ill|Awaji Island|en|Awaji Island|qid=Q504373|lt=Awaji Island}} these are referred to as either “{{ill|futon danjiri|ja|ふとんだんじり}}” or “{{ill|kaki(gi) danjiri|ja|かき（ぎ）だんじり}}”. Although no one has catalogued every surviving example on the island, it is estimated that roughly 200 exist. For ease of movement during festivals, wheels are attached to the base. In southern Awaji the wheels are primarily used to rock the platform like a seesaw or to enable simple rotation; in some areas a rudder ({{ill|Rudder|en|Rudder|qid=Q209760|lt=teji}} or 梃子) is attached to facilitate handling during rotation or towing. In many cases the offering to the shrine is conceived as a pair with {{ill|Jōruri (music)|en|Jōruri (music)|qid=Q1361891|lt=jōruri}}. Local youth repeatedly rehearse prior to the festival and often perform futon taiko songs. In northern Awaji, by contrast, the wheels are removed during the parade ({{ill|Shinko-shiki|ja|宮入|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/miyairi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 神幸祭|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 神幸祭|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q123907414}}) so that the platform is carried; here the emphasis is on the martial grandeur and competitive spirit of the carrying.

*Sakai Type  
:In the Sakai type, the entire futon taiko is elaborately carved with depictions of mythology, human sentiment, landscapes, and flora and fauna; carvings extend onto the door panels and railings. Here the futon’s thickness increases from the bottom upward and the angle is relatively small; moreover, instead of a golden rope, a material such as {{ill|Rasha|ja|羅紗|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Rasha|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ラシャ|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ラシャ|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11346737}} is used for binding. Its most prominent feature is that beneath the futon a futon platform with a small roof is attached, and even the supporting pillars—extending fully to the ground—are made from a single continuous piece of wood (four integrated columns).

*Shell Mound Type  
:In this variation, in place of the decorative knots or dragonfly motifs, an element known as “{{ill|māra|ja|魔羅|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/mara|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 魔|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 魔|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q15726943}}” stands upright. The base shows intricate carvings reminiscent of those on the base wheels, and the pillars can slide vertically—a feature known as “{{ill|seriage|ja|せり上げ}}.”

*Mountain-type Futon Floats  
:These are common in areas such as {{ill|Takasago, Hyōgo|en|Takasago, Hyōgo|qid=Q869037|lt=Takasago City}}, the northern parts of {{ill|Kakogawa, Hyōgo|en|Kakogawa, Hyōgo|qid=Q750569|lt=Kakogawa City}}, and the northern region of the former {{ill|Harima|en|Harima|qid=Q3783364|lt=Harima}}.

'''{{ill|Aguchi Shrine|ja|開口神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kaikō Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11655187}} Hassaku Festival''' (on the Friday preceding the first Golden Day, Saturday, and Sunday)  
In {{ill|泉州 (disambiguation)|en|泉州 (disambiguation)|qid=Q11143129|lt=Senshū}}, the original Hassaku Festival featured futon taiko even before their formal dedication, with a history of about 600 years. At its peak, as many as 13 taiko platforms were paraded.
* Ashiharahama  
* Dainantogawa/Sumida (Sakai-type)  
* Shinzaike-hama  
* Daikōhama  
(Note: In the 10th anniversary refurbishment, Daikōhama was changed to a futon taiko with red and white futon.)
* Additionally, child taiko from Minamihanmachi also participate.  
* Daikōhama was revived after a hiatus of about 70 years by local volunteers.  
* From September 8, 2024, the Dainantogawa Sumida Youth Association was renamed the Dainantogawa Sumida Taiko Association.
'''{{ill|Sugawara Shrine|ja|菅原神社 (堺市)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sugawara Shrine (Sakai)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11619211}} Hassaku Festival''' (on the Friday preceding the first Golden Day, Saturday, and Sunday)  
* {{ill|Kaishenhama|ja|海船濱}} (Sakai-type)  
* {{ill|Kitatogawa|ja|北戸川}} (Sakai-type)  
Child taiko from Kitatogawa also participate.
* Until 2017 ({{ill|2017|en|2017|qid=Q25290|lt=Heisei 29}}), taiko platforms were typically paraded on September 13–15; however, due to lower participation and spectator numbers on weekdays compared to weekends, from 2018 ({{ill|2018|en|2018|qid=Q25291|lt=Heisei 30}}) the schedule was changed to match that of the Kaikō Shrine Hassaku Festival (Friday preceding Golden Day, Saturday, and Sunday).  
* Before World War II, as many as 14 taiko platforms were paraded during the peak; subsequently, due to air raids and a shortage of carriers, many were abolished, and currently only 2 remain in the parade.  
* In addition to futon taiko, Kitatogawa also features a lion dance called “{{ill|Togawa no Shishi|ja|戸川之獅子}}” which, aside from the Hassaku Festival, also appears at local Bon festivals and in events held in parks and schools.
'''{{ill|Futondaiko Matsuri (Osaka)|ja|ふとん太鼓台祭}}'''  
(Third Friday, Saturday, and Sunday of September)  
* Ishizutsukawamukai Alliance (comprising groups from Ishizutsukawamukai, Ishizuhigashi, Ishizuwakanaka, Kitawakanaka, Jūsanchō-kai, and Nishidōzō-kai)  
* Enoki  
* Dainantogawa Sumida Youth Association  
* Kitatogawa  
* Shinzaike-hama  
* Daikōhama  
* (Ishizutsukawamukai participates once every three years selected from among six towns)
* Additionally, besides the taiko platforms, child taiko from Nankōmachi used to participate; however, they were once donated to Sakai City and later given to Calabasas, USA.

* Ishizutsukawamukai Alliance (Ishizutsukawamukai, Ishizuhigashi, Ishizuwakanaka, Kitawakanaka, Jūsanchō-kai, Nishidōzō-kai)

== (The article continues with sections on futon taiko in other regions – such as in Sakai City, Kaizuka City, Izumisano City, Ibaraki City, Nara City, and elsewhere – as well as historical notes, chants and shouts, details on preserved and abolished taiko platforms, and further regional variations.) ==
== History ==
The futon taiko of the former {{ill|Sakai|en|Sakai|qid=Q193428|lt=Sakai City}} are said to have been carried as early as the mid-Edo period during the festivals of {{ill|Sumiyoshi-taisha|de|Sumiyoshi-Taisha|es|Sumiyoshi Taisha|fa|سومییوشی-تایشا|fi|Sumiyoshi-taisha|fr|Sumiyoshi-taisha|it|Grande santuario di Sumiyoshi|ja|住吉大社|ko|스미요시 대사|la|Sumiyoshi-taisha|my|ဆုမိရောရှိနန်းကွန်းနန်းရင်း|pt|Sumiyoshi taisha|ru|Сумиёси-тайся|sl|Veliko svetišče Sumijoši-taiša|th|ศาลเจ้าซูมิโยชิ|tr|Sumiyoshi-taisha|uk|Сумійосі тайся|zh|住吉大社|qid=Q705949|lt=Sumiyoshi Taisha}}, as depicted on the “{{nihongo|Mimura Miyamatsuri Ema|ja|三村宮祭礼絵馬|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mimura Miyamatsuri Ema|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}.” In Sakai City, until roughly the mid-Meiji period, during festivals each parishioner group would pull floats and halberds, and taiko platforms existed as part of the ritual. However, on a festival held on August 1 (old calendar) in {{ill|1896|en|1896|qid=Q7846|lt=Meiji 29}}, on a narrow section of the {{ill|Kishū Kaidō|ja|紀州街道|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kishu Highway|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11605050}} in Nakanomachi West (narrow enough for only one float), a collision occurred between a boat float from the Minato group and a float from the northern blacksmith district, resulting in a dispute and casualties. This incident, known as the “Sakai Float Incident,” led to a complete ban on parading elaborately decorated floats in the (old) Sakai area thereafter.
Later, to celebrate Japan’s victory in the {{ill|Russo-Japanese War|en|Russo-Japanese War|qid=Q159950|lt=Russo-Japanese War}}, the parading of elaborately decorated floats was permitted again; however, because parishioners disposed of or sold their floats, many float craftsmen left Sakai or changed trades, and because of safety concerns and the fact that many regions began purchasing futon taiko from {{ill|Awaji|en|Awaji|qid=Q349322|lt=Awaji}}, only the futon taiko remained.
In the {{ill|Taishō era|ja|大正時代|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Taishō period|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大正|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大正|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q329174}}, at {{ill|Aguchi Shrine|ja|開口神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kaikō Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11655187}} as many as 13 taiko platforms and at {{ill|Sugawara Shrine|ja|菅原神社 (堺市)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sugawara Shrine (Sakai)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11619211}} as many as 14 were offered, marking the golden age of Sakai’s futon taiko. Each district showcased its individuality through unique decorative features—such as non-white tassels, embroidered futon coverings (with, for example, Shinzaike-hama still using blue), and variations in tying methods.
In the {{ill|Shōwa era|en|Shōwa era|qid=Q327567|lt=Shōwa period}} labor shortages and other circumstances led some parishioners to relinquish their taiko platforms; later, many futon taiko were destroyed in the {{ill|Bombing of Osaka|ja|堺大空襲|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sakai Air Raid|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大阪大空襲|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大阪大空襲|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q2814395}}. In the postwar period, due to material shortages, decoration reverted to a basic style; however, in recent years there has been a revival of the lavish prewar style.
Since 1974, futon taiko have participated in the {{ill|Sakai Matsuri|en|Sakai Matsuri|qid=Q11428095|lt=Sakai Festival}} and its eve festival. Initially only those from Ashiharahama, Dainantogawa, Kitatogawa, and Shinzaike-hama participated; later 10 districts joined. All these taiko platforms are members of the {{ill|Sakai Festival Futon Taiko Preservation Union|ja|堺まつりふとん太鼓連合保存会|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sakai Festival Futon Taiko Preservation Union|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11428096}}.
* Note: Ashiharahama, Dejima, Nishiminato, and Higashiminato withdrew in 2019.
In 1991, Ashiharahama, in 1993 Dejima, and in 2002 the Ishizutsukawamukai (specifically Ishizuwakanaka) represented the union in the {{ill|Midosuji Parade|ja|御堂筋パレード|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Midosuji Parade|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11488902}}.
On May 1, 2019, a commemorative ceremony was held at {{ill|Daisen Park|ja|大仙公園}}, centered on the Sakai Festival Futon Taiko Preservation Union, to mark the accession of the new Emperor. A total of 11 taiko platforms (from Ishizutsukawamukai, Enoki, Dainantogawa, Enokicho, Kaishenhama, Kitatogawa, Shinzaike-hama, Daikōhama, Nishiminato, Hamaishi, and Higashiminato) participated. The ceremony also saw participation from districts (such as Enokicho, Kaishenhama, and Hamaishi) that do not normally take part in the Sakai Festival.
Due to the impact of the {{ill|Novel coronavirus|en|Novel coronavirus|qid=Q84497971|lt=novel coronavirus}}, in 2020 and 2021 the parading of taiko platforms was suspended in various regions.

【Carrying Call】  
"Yoitoyaiyamaka, Dokkoisa-no-se  
(Sōryā – dekita! Dekita!)"
【Festival Song】
*Verse 1*  
"Autumn moon over {{ill|Ishiyama|ja|石山|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ishiyama|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q15890429}},  
Clouds gather amid the flowers borne by the wind;  
The news carried by the wind comes from the island of {{ill|Q11657489|ja|阿波|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Awa|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11657489}},  
And in a striped wallet, five or ten ryo;  
What is that rumbling sound?  
After earthquakes and thunder comes the evening shower—  
Berabera, berashoshoshoi!"
*Verse 2*  
"Peonies with Chinese lion motifs,  
Bamboo where tigers chase—  
In pursuit of the noble one, lending wisdom;  
At {{ill|Seikan-ji Temple|ja|中山清閑寺|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chūzan Seikan-ji|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|qid=Q135490861}},  
The resident of Seikan-ji is a monk,  
Thus it is the Hassaku rain—  
Berabera, berashoshoshoi!"  
*(In some districts the line “Thus it is the Hassaku rain” is omitted.)*
*Verse 3*  
*(Once sung mainly in the old city district; currently preserved only in select areas such as Kaishenhama.)*
In addition, many districts have their own original festival songs.
【Victory Shout】  
"Yāe, Yāe, Āyoiyamakasokojaina, Yōiyase!"

== Abolished Futon Taiko ==
Due to air raids during the {{ill|World War II|en|World War II|qid=Q362|lt=Second World War}} and postwar carrier shortages, many taiko platforms were abolished.  
At the peak in the old city district there were roughly 30 district groups’ worth of futon taiko—comparable to the total number now in Sakai City.

[[File:Night in Kaizuka Taiko Platform.jpg|thumb|A Kaizuka taiko platform decorated with lanterns. In recent years, the South Taiko has also adopted a light-up method from {{ill|2017|en|2017|qid=Q25290|lt=Heisei 29}}; however, from a traditional standpoint some oppose imitating other regions. In the second year, the evening uses “lanterns” while the main shrine uses “light-up.”|alt=|left|283x283px]]
[[File:0minaminisi.jpg|thumb|In {{ill|1919|ja|大正八年|2=ja|3=1919年|lt=Taishō 8|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Taishō 8|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q2157}} at the main shrine in {{ill|Kaizuka Hama|ja|貝塚浜}}, a newly refurbished West Taiko Platform is shown (note that the belt is still white at first and turns black over subsequent years). This is a masterpiece by {{ill|Yoshikuni Sakurai|ja|桜井義国|qid=Q140445971}}, executed with full vigor. The left platform is the lost predecessor South Taiko (said to have been burned in a warehouse fire due to a plague outbreak).|alt=|left|286x286px]]
The Hassaku Festival at {{ill|Kanda Shrine|ja|感田神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kaizuka Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11494969}} (officially “{{ill|Kaizuka Miya Taiko Platform Festival|ja|貝塚宮太鼓台祭}}”) is held on the Friday immediately preceding Golden Day, Saturday, and Sunday. In {{ill|泉州 (disambiguation)|en|泉州 (disambiguation)|qid=Q11143129|lt=Senshū}}, the original Hassaku Festival featured futon taiko long before their formal dedication, with a history of about 600 years. At its peak, 13 taiko platforms were paraded.
* Ashiharahama  
* Dainantogawa/Sumida (Sakai-type)  
* Shinzaike-hama  
* Daikōhama  
(Note: At one time, Daikōhama was converted to a futon taiko with red and white futon during its 10th-anniversary refurbishment.)
* Additionally, child taiko from Minamihanmachi participate.  
* Daikōhama was revived after roughly 70 years by local volunteers.  
* From September 8, 2024, the Dainantogawa Sumida Youth Association was renamed the Dainantogawa Sumida Taiko Association.
'''{{ill|Sugawara Shrine|ja|菅原神社 (堺市)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sugawara Shrine (Sakai)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11619211}} Hassaku Festival''' (held on the Friday immediately preceding Golden Day, Saturday, and Sunday)  
* {{ill|Kaishenhama|ja|海船濱}} (Sakai-type)  
* {{ill|Kitatogawa|ja|北戸川}} (Sakai-type)  
Child taiko from Kitatogawa also participate.
* Until 2017 ({{ill|2017|en|2017|qid=Q25290|lt=Heisei 29}}) taiko platforms were typically paraded on September 13–15; however, due to lower participation on weekdays compared to holidays, from 2018 ({{ill|2018|en|2018|qid=Q25291|lt=Heisei 30}}) the schedule was changed to match that of the Kaikō Shrine Hassaku Festival (Friday preceding Golden Day, Saturday, and Sunday).  
* Before World War II, as many as 14 taiko platforms were paraded at the peak; later, many were abolished due to air raids and a shortage of carriers, and currently only 2 are paraded.
* In addition to futon taiko, Kitatogawa also features a lion dance known as “{{ill|Togawa no Shishi|ja|戸川之獅子}}” which, apart from the Hassaku Festival, also appears at local Bon festivals and at park and school events.

== (Additional sections follow for taiko platforms in other cities such as Izumisano, Ibaraki, Nara, and further regions; as well as sections on history, chants, preserved and abolished platforms, and related external links.) ==
== History ==
The futon taiko of the former {{ill|Sakai|en|Sakai|qid=Q193428|lt=Sakai City}} are said to have been carried as early as the mid-Edo period during the festivals of {{ill|Sumiyoshi-taisha|de|Sumiyoshi-Taisha|es|Sumiyoshi Taisha|fa|سومییوشی-تایشا|fi|Sumiyoshi-taisha|fr|Sumiyoshi-taisha|it|Grande santuario di Sumiyoshi|ja|住吉大社|ko|스미요시 대사|la|Sumiyoshi-taisha|my|ဆုမိရောရှိနန်းကွန်းနန်းရင်း|pt|Sumiyoshi taisha|ru|Сумиёси-тайся|sl|Veliko svetišče Sumijoši-taiša|th|ศาลเจ้าซูมิโยชิ|tr|Sumiyoshi-taisha|uk|Сумійосі тайся|zh|住吉大社|qid=Q705949|lt=Sumiyoshi Taisha}}, as depicted on the “{{nihongo|Mimura Miyamatsuri Ema|ja|三村宮祭礼絵馬|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mimura Miyamatsuri Ema|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}.” In Sakai City, until roughly the mid-Meiji period, during festivals each local parishioner group would pull floats and halberds, and taiko platforms were integral to the ritual. However, on a festival held on August 1 (old calendar) in {{ill|1896|en|1896|qid=Q7846|lt=Meiji 29}}, on a narrow section of the {{ill|Kishū Kaidō|ja|紀州街道|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kishu Highway|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11605050}} in Nakanomachi West (narrow enough for only one float), a collision occurred between a boat float from the Minato group and a float from the northern blacksmith district, resulting in a dispute and casualties. This incident, known as the “Sakai Float Incident,” led to a complete ban on parading elaborately decorated floats in the old Sakai area thereafter.
Later, to celebrate Japan’s victory in the {{ill|Russo-Japanese War|en|Russo-Japanese War|qid=Q159950|lt=Russo-Japanese War}}, the parading of elaborately decorated floats was permitted again; however, because parishioners disposed of or sold their floats, many float craftsmen left Sakai or changed trades, and concerns over safety—and the fact that many regions began purchasing futon taiko from {{ill|Awaji|en|Awaji|qid=Q349322|lt=Awaji}}—resulted in only futon taiko remaining.
In the {{ill|Taishō era|ja|大正時代|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Taishō period|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大正|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大正|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q329174}}, at {{ill|Aguchi Shrine|ja|開口神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kaikō Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11655187}} as many as 13 taiko platforms and at {{ill|Sugawara Shrine|ja|菅原神社 (堺市)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sugawara Shrine (Sakai)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11619211}} as many as 14 were offered, marking the golden age of Sakai’s futon taiko. Each district expressed its individuality through unique decorative features—such as tassels in colors other than white, embroidered futon coverings (for instance, Shinzaike-hama still uses blue), and varied tying methods.
In the {{ill|Shōwa era|en|Shōwa era|qid=Q327567|lt=Shōwa period}}, due to labor shortages and other factors, some parishioners began to relinquish their taiko platforms, and later many futon taiko were lost in the {{ill|Bombing of Osaka|ja|堺大空襲|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sakai Air Raid|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大阪大空襲|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大阪大空襲|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q2814395}}. In the postwar period, because of material shortages, decorations reverted to a basic style; however, in recent years there has been a revival toward the lavish prewar style.
Since 1974, futon taiko have participated in the {{ill|Sakai Matsuri|en|Sakai Matsuri|qid=Q11428095|lt=Sakai Festival}} and its eve festival. Initially, only those from Ashiharahama, Dainantogawa, Kitatogawa, and Shinzaike-hama participated; later, 10 district groups joined. All these taiko platforms are members of the {{ill|Sakai Festival Futon Taiko Preservation Union|ja|堺まつりふとん太鼓連合保存会|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sakai Festival Futon Taiko Preservation Union|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11428096}}.
* Note: Ashiharahama, Dejima, Nishiminato, and Higashiminato withdrew in 2019.
In 1991, Ashiharahama; in 1993, Dejima; and in 2002, the Ishizutsukawamukai (specifically Ishizuwakanaka) represented the union in the {{ill|Midosuji Parade|ja|御堂筋パレード|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Midosuji Parade|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11488902}}.
On May 1, 2019, a commemorative ceremony was held at {{ill|Daisen Park|ja|大仙公園}}, centered on the Sakai Festival Futon Taiko Preservation Union, to mark the accession of the new Emperor. A total of 11 taiko platforms (from Ishizutsukawamukai, Enoki, Dainantogawa, Enokicho, Kaishenhama, Kitatogawa, Shinzaike-hama, Daikōhama, Nishiminato, Hamaishi, and Higashiminato) participated. The ceremony also saw participation from districts (such as Enokicho, Kaishenhama, and Hamaishi) that do not normally participate in the Sakai Festival.
Due to the impact of the {{ill|Novel coronavirus|en|Novel coronavirus|qid=Q84497971|lt=novel coronavirus}}, in 2020 and 2021 the parading of taiko platforms was suspended in various regions.

"Autumn moon over {{ill|Ishiyama|ja|石山|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ishiyama|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q15890429}},  
Clouds cluster about, and blossoms ride on the wind;  
News travels on the breeze from the island of {{ill|Q11657489|ja|阿波|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Awa|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11657489}},  
In a striped wallet, five or ten ryo;  
What is that rumbling sound?  
After earthquakes and thunder, the evening shower comes—  
Berabera, berashoshoshoi!"
*Verse 2*  
"Peonies with Chinese lion motifs,  
Bamboo chased by tigers—  
Chasing the noble one, lending wisdom;  
At {{ill|Seikan-ji Temple|ja|中山清閑寺|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chūzan Seikan-ji|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|qid=Q135490861}},

Thus it is the Hassaku rain—  
Berabera, berashoshoshoi!"

*Verse 3*

== (Additional sections follow for taiko platforms in other cities such as Izumisano, Ibaraki, Nara, and further regions; as well as sections on history, chants, preserved and abolished platforms, and related external links.) ==
== History ==
The futon taiko of the former {{ill|Sakai|en|Sakai|qid=Q193428|lt=Sakai City}} are said to have been carried as early as the mid-Edo period during the festivals of {{ill|Sumiyoshi-taisha|de|Sumiyoshi-Taisha|es|Sumiyoshi Taisha|fa|سومییوشی-تایشا|fi|Sumiyoshi-taisha|fr|Sumiyoshi-taisha|it|Grande santuario di Sumiyoshi|ja|住吉大社|ko|스미요시 대사|la|Sumiyoshi-taisha|my|ဆုမိရောရှိနန်းကွန်းနန်းရင်း|pt|Sumiyoshi taisha|ru|Сумиёси-тайся|sl|Veliko svetišče Sumijoši-taiša|th|ศาลเจ้าซูมิโยชิ|tr|Sumiyoshi-taisha|uk|Сумійосі тайся|zh|住吉大社|qid=Q705949|lt=Sumiyoshi Taisha}}, as depicted on the “{{nihongo|Mimura Miyamatsuri Ema|ja|三村宮祭礼絵馬|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mimura Miyamatsuri Ema|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}.” In Sakai City, until roughly the mid-Meiji period, each local parishioner group would pull floats and halberds during festivals, and taiko platforms were integral to the ritual. However, on a festival held on August 1 (old calendar) in {{ill|1896|en|1896|qid=Q7846|lt=Meiji 29}}, on a narrow section of the {{ill|Kishū Kaidō|ja|紀州街道|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kishu Highway|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11605050}} in Nakanomachi West (narrow enough for only one float), a collision occurred between a boat float from the Minato group and a float from the northern blacksmith district, resulting in a dispute and casualties. This incident, known as the “Sakai Float Incident,” led to a complete ban on parading elaborately decorated floats in the old Sakai area thereafter.
Later, to celebrate Japan’s victory in the {{ill|Russo-Japanese War|en|Russo-Japanese War|qid=Q159950|lt=Russo-Japanese War}}, the parading of elaborately decorated floats was permitted again; however, because parishioners disposed of or sold their floats, many float craftsmen left Sakai or changed trades, and concerns over safety—and the fact that many regions began purchasing futon taiko from {{ill|Awaji|en|Awaji|qid=Q349322|lt=Awaji}}—resulted in only futon taiko remaining.
In the {{ill|Taishō era|ja|大正時代|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Taishō period|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大正|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大正|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q329174}}, at {{ill|Aguchi Shrine|ja|開口神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kaikō Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11655187}} as many as 13 taiko platforms and at {{ill|Sugawara Shrine|ja|菅原神社 (堺市)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sugawara Shrine (Sakai)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11619211}} as many as 14 were offered, marking the golden age of Sakai’s futon taiko. Each district expressed its individuality through unique decorative features—such as tassels in colors other than white, embroidered futon coverings (for example, Shinzaike-hama still uses blue), and varied tying methods.
In the {{ill|Shōwa era|en|Shōwa era|qid=Q327567|lt=Shōwa period}}, due to labor shortages and other circumstances, some parishioners began relinquishing their taiko platforms, and later many futon taiko were lost in the {{ill|Bombing of Osaka|ja|堺大空襲|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sakai Air Raid|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大阪大空襲|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大阪大空襲|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q2814395}}. In the postwar period, because of material shortages, decoration reverted to a basic style; however, in recent years there has been a revival toward the lavish prewar style.
Since 1974, futon taiko have participated in the {{ill|Sakai Matsuri|en|Sakai Matsuri|qid=Q11428095|lt=Sakai Festival}} and its eve festival. Initially, only those from Ashiharahama, Dainantogawa, Kitatogawa, and Shinzaike-hama participated; later, 10 district groups joined. All these taiko platforms are members of the {{ill|Sakai Festival Futon Taiko Preservation Union|ja|堺まつりふとん太鼓連合保存会|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sakai Festival Futon Taiko Preservation Union|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11428096}}.
* Note: Ashiharahama, Dejima, Nishiminato, and Higashiminato withdrew in 2019.
In 1991, Ashiharahama; in 1993, Dejima; and in 2002, the Ishizutsukawamukai (specifically Ishizuwakanaka) represented the union in the {{ill|Midosuji Parade|ja|御堂筋パレード|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Midosuji Parade|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11488902}}.
On May 1, 2019, a commemorative ceremony was held at {{ill|Daisen Park|ja|大仙公園}}, centered on the Sakai Festival Futon Taiko Preservation Union, to mark the accession of the new Emperor. Eleven taiko platforms (from Ishizutsukawamukai, Enoki, Dainantogawa, Enokicho, Kaishenhama, Kitatogawa, Shinzaike-hama, Daikōhama, Nishiminato, Hamaishi, and Higashiminato) participated. The ceremony also saw participation from districts (such as Enokicho, Kaishenhama, and Hamaishi) that do not normally participate in the Sakai Festival.
Due to the impact of the {{ill|Novel coronavirus|en|Novel coronavirus|qid=Q84497971|lt=novel coronavirus}}, in 2020 and 2021 the parading of taiko platforms was suspended in various regions.

This incident, known as the “Sakai Float Incident,” led to a complete ban on parading elaborately decorated floats in the old Sakai area thereafter.
Later, to celebrate Japan’s victory in the {{ill|Russo-Japanese War|en|Russo-Japanese War|qid=Q159950|lt=Russo-Japanese War}}, the parading of elaborately decorated floats was permitted again; however, because parishioners disposed of or sold their floats, many float craftsmen left Sakai or changed trades, and concerns over safety—and the fact that many regions began purchasing futon taiko from {{ill|Awaji|en|Awaji|qid=Q349322|lt=Awaji}}—resulted in only futon taiko remaining.
In the {{ill|Taishō era|ja|大正時代|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Taishō period|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大正|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大正|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q329174}}, at {{ill|Aguchi Shrine|ja|開口神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kaikō Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11655187}} as many as 13 taiko platforms and at {{ill|Sugawara Shrine|ja|菅原神社 (堺市)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sugawara Shrine (Sakai)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11619211}} as many as 14 were offered, marking the golden age of Sakai’s futon taiko. Each district expressed its individuality through unique decorative features—such as tassels in colors other than white, embroidered futon coverings (for example, Shinzaike-hama still uses blue), and varied tying methods.
In the {{ill|Shōwa era|en|Shōwa era|qid=Q327567|lt=Shōwa period}}, due to labor shortages and other circumstances, some parishioners began relinquishing their taiko platforms, and later many futon taiko were lost in the {{ill|Bombing of Osaka|ja|堺大空襲|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sakai Air Raid|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大阪大空襲|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大阪大空襲|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q2814395}}. In the postwar period, because of material shortages, decoration reverted to a basic style; however, in recent years there has been a revival toward the lavish prewar style.
Since 1974, futon taiko have participated in the {{ill|Sakai Matsuri|en|Sakai Matsuri|qid=Q11428095|lt=Sakai Festival}} and its eve festival. Initially, only those from Ashiharahama, Dainantogawa, Kitatogawa, and Shinzaike-hama participated; later, 10 district groups joined. All these taiko platforms are members of the {{ill|Sakai Festival Futon Taiko Preservation Union|ja|堺まつりふとん太鼓連合保存会|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sakai Festival Futon Taiko Preservation Union|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11428096}}.
* Note: Ashiharahama, Dejima, Nishiminato, and Higashiminato withdrew in 2019.
In 1991, Ashiharahama; in 1993, Dejima; and in 2002, the Ishizutsukawamukai (specifically Ishizuwakanaka) represented the union in the {{ill|Midosuji Parade|ja|御堂筋パレード|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Midosuji Parade|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11488902}}.
On May 1, 2019, a commemorative ceremony was held at {{ill|Daisen Park|ja|大仙公園}}, centered on the Sakai Festival Futon Taiko Preservation Union, to mark the accession of the new Emperor. Eleven taiko platforms (from Ishizutsukawamukai, Enoki, Dainantogawa, Enokicho, Kaishenhama, Kitatogawa, Shinzaike-hama, Daikōhama, Nishiminato, Hamaishi, and Higashiminato) participated. The ceremony also saw participation from districts (such as Enokicho, Kaishenhama, and Hamaishi) that do not normally participate in the Sakai Festival.
Due to the impact of the {{ill|Novel coronavirus|en|Novel coronavirus|qid=Q84497971|lt=novel coronavirus}}, in 2020 and 2021 the parading of taiko platforms was suspended in various regions.

== Abolished Futon Taiko ==

== Taiko Platforms in Kaizuka City ==
'''''{{ill|Kanda Shrine|ja|感田神社}} Summer Festival (Adult Taiko Platforms) • Autumn Festival (Child Taiko)'''''  
[[File:Night in Kaizuka Taiko Platform.jpg|thumb|A Kaizuka taiko platform decorated with lanterns. In recent years, the South Taiko has also adopted a light-up method from {{ill|2017|en|2017|qid=Q25290|lt=Heisei 29}}; however, from a traditional viewpoint some oppose imitating other regions. In the second year, the evening uses “lanterns” while the main shrine uses “light-up.”|alt=|left|283x283px]]
[[File:0minaminisi.jpg|thumb|In {{ill|1919|ja|大正八年|2=ja|3=1919年|lt=Taishō 8|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Taishō 8|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q2157}} at the main shrine of {{ill|Kaizuka Hama|ja|貝塚浜}}, a newly refurbished West Taiko Platform is shown (note that the belt is initially white and turns black over subsequent years). This is a masterpiece by {{ill|Yoshikuni Sakurai|ja|桜井義国|qid=Q140445971}}, executed with full vigor. The left platform is the lost predecessor South Taiko (said to have been burned in a warehouse fire due to a plague outbreak).|alt=|left|286x286px]]
The Hassaku Festival at {{ill|Kanda Shrine|ja|感田神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kaizuka Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11494969}} (officially “{{ill|Kaizuka Miya Taiko Platform Festival|ja|貝塚宮太鼓台祭}}”) is held on the Friday immediately preceding Golden Day, Saturday, and Sunday. In {{ill|泉州 (disambiguation)|en|泉州 (disambiguation)|qid=Q11143129|lt=Senshū}}, the original Hassaku Festival featured futon taiko even before their formal dedication, with a history of about 600 years. At its peak, 13 taiko platforms were paraded.
* Ashiharahama  
* Dainantogawa/Sumida (Sakai-type)  
* Shinzaike-hama  
* Daikōhama  
(Note: At one time, Daikōhama was converted to a futon taiko with red and white futon during its 10th-anniversary refurbishment.)
* Additionally, child taiko from Minamihanmachi participate.  
* Daikōhama was revived after roughly 70 years by local volunteers.  
* From September 8, 2024, the Dainantogawa Sumida Youth Association has been renamed the Dainantogawa Sumida Taiko Association.
'''{{ill|Sugawara Shrine|ja|菅原神社 (堺市)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sugawara Shrine (Sakai)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11619211}} Hassaku Festival''' (held on the Friday immediately preceding Golden Day, Saturday, and Sunday)  
* {{ill|Kaishenhama|ja|海船濱}} (Sakai-type)  
* {{ill|Kitatogawa|ja|北戸川}} (Sakai-type)  
Child taiko from Kitatogawa also participate.
* Until 2017 ({{ill|2017|en|2017|qid=Q25290|lt=Heisei 29}}) taiko platforms were typically paraded on September 13–15; however, due to lower turnout on weekdays compared to holidays, from 2018 ({{ill|2018|en|2018|qid=Q25291|lt=Heisei 30}}) the schedule was changed to match that of the Kaikō Shrine Hassaku Festival (Friday preceding Golden Day, Saturday, and Sunday).  
* Before World War II, as many as 14 taiko platforms were paraded at the peak; subsequently, many were abolished due to air raids and a shortage of carriers, and currently only 2 are paraded.
* In addition to futon taiko, Kitatogawa also features a lion dance called “{{ill|Togawa no Shishi|ja|戸川之獅子}}” which, aside from the Hassaku Festival, also appears at local Bon festivals and in park or school events.

== (Additional sections follow for taiko platforms in other cities such as Izumisano, Ibaraki, Nara, and further regions; as well as sections on history, chants, preserved and abolished platforms, and related external links.) ==
== History ==
The futon taiko of the former {{ill|Sakai|en|Sakai|qid=Q193428|lt=Sakai City}} are said to have been carried as early as the mid-Edo period during the festivals of {{ill|Sumiyoshi-taisha|de|Sumiyoshi-Taisha|es|Sumiyoshi Taisha|fa|سومییوشی-تایشا|fi|Sumiyoshi-taisha|fr|Sumiyoshi-taisha|it|Grande santuario di Sumiyoshi|ja|住吉大社|ko|스미요시 대사|la|Sumiyoshi-taisha|my|ဆုမိရောရှိနန်းကွန်းနန်းရင်း|pt|Sumiyoshi taisha|ru|Сумиёси-тайся|sl|Veliko svetišče Sumijoši-taiša|th|ศาลเจ้าซูมิโยชิ|tr|Sumiyoshi-taisha|uk|Сумійосі тайся|zh|住吉大社|qid=Q705949|lt=Sumiyoshi Taisha}}, as depicted on the “{{nihongo|Mimura Miyamatsuri Ema|ja|三村宮祭礼絵馬|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mimura Miyamatsuri Ema|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}.” In Sakai City, until roughly the mid-Meiji period, each local parishioner group would pull floats and halberds during festivals, and taiko platforms were integral to the ritual. However, on a festival held on August 1 (old calendar) in {{ill|1896|en|1896|qid=Q7846|lt=Meiji 29}}, on a narrow section of the {{ill|Kishū Kaidō|ja|紀州街道|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kishu Highway|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11605050}} in Nakanomachi West (narrow enough for only one float), a collision occurred between a boat float from the Minato group and a float from the northern blacksmith district, resulting in a dispute and casualties. This incident, known as the “Sakai Float Incident,” led to a complete ban on parading elaborately decorated floats in the old Sakai area thereafter.
Later, to celebrate Japan’s victory in the {{ill|Russo-Japanese War|en|Russo-Japanese War|qid=Q159950|lt=Russo-Japanese War}}, the parading of elaborately decorated floats was permitted again; however, because parishioners disposed of or sold their floats, many float craftsmen left Sakai or changed trades, and concerns over safety—and the fact that many regions began purchasing futon taiko from {{ill|Awaji|en|Awaji|qid=Q349322|lt=Awaji}}—resulted in only futon taiko remaining.
In the {{ill|Taishō era|ja|大正時代|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Taishō period|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大正|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大正|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q329174}}, at {{ill|Aguchi Shrine|ja|開口神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kaikō Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11655187}} as many as 13 taiko platforms and at {{ill|Sugawara Shrine|ja|菅原神社 (堺市)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sugawara Shrine (Sakai)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11619211}} as many as 14 were offered, marking the golden age of Sakai’s futon taiko. Each district expressed its individuality through unique decorative features—such as tassels in colors other than white, embroidered futon coverings (for example, Shinzaike-hama still uses blue), and varied tying methods.
In the {{ill|Shōwa era|en|Shōwa era|qid=Q327567|lt=Shōwa period}}, due to labor shortages and other circumstances, some parishioners began relinquishing their taiko platforms, and later many futon taiko were lost in the {{ill|Bombing of Osaka|ja|堺大空襲|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sakai Air Raid|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大阪大空襲|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大阪大空襲|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q2814395}}. In the postwar period, because of material shortages, decoration reverted to a basic style; however, in recent years there has been a revival toward the lavish prewar style.
Since 1974, futon taiko have participated in the {{ill|Sakai Matsuri|en|Sakai Matsuri|qid=Q11428095|lt=Sakai Festival}} and its eve festival. Initially, only those from Ashiharahama, Dainantogawa, Kitatogawa, and Shinzaike-hama participated; later, 10 district groups joined. All these taiko platforms are members of the {{ill|Sakai Festival Futon Taiko Preservation Union|ja|堺まつりふとん太鼓連合保存会|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sakai Festival Futon Taiko Preservation Union|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11428096}}.
* Note: Ashiharahama, Dejima, Nishiminato, and Higashiminato withdrew in 2019.
In 1991, Ashiharahama; in 1993, Dejima; and in 2002, the Ishizutsukawamukai (specifically Ishizuwakanaka) represented the union in the {{ill|Midosuji Parade|ja|御堂筋パレード|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Midosuji Parade|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11488902}}.
On May 1, 2019, a commemorative ceremony was held at {{ill|Daisen Park|ja|大仙公園}}, centered on the Sakai Festival Futon Taiko Preservation Union, to mark the accession of the new Emperor. Eleven taiko platforms (from Ishizutsukawamukai, Enoki, Dainantogawa, Enokicho, Kaishenhama, Kitatogawa, Shinzaike-hama, Daikōhama, Nishiminato, Hamaishi, and Higashiminato) participated. The ceremony also saw participation from districts (such as Enokicho, Kaishenhama, and Hamaishi) that do not normally participate in the Sakai Festival.
Due to the impact of the {{ill|Novel coronavirus|en|Novel coronavirus|qid=Q84497971|lt=novel coronavirus}}, in 2020 and 2021 the parading of taiko platforms was suspended in various regions.

【Festival Song】

"Autumn moon over {{ill|Ishiyama|ja|石山|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ishiyama|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q15890429}},  
Clouds cluster and blossoms ride upon the wind;  
News travels on the breeze from the island of {{ill|Q11657489|ja|阿波|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Awa|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11657489}},  
In a striped wallet, five or ten ryo;

After earthquakes and thunder, the evening shower comes—  
Berabera, berashoshoshoi!"
*Verse 2*  
"Peonies with Chinese lion motifs,  
Bamboo pursued by tigers—  
Chasing the noble one, lending wisdom;  
At {{ill|Seikan-ji Temple|ja|中山清閑寺|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chūzan Seikan-ji|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|qid=Q135490861}},

Thus it is the Hassaku rain—  
Berabera, berashoshoshoi!"

*Verse 3*

In addition, many districts have their own original festival songs.

== Abolished Futon Taiko ==
Due to air raids during the {{ill|World War II|en|World War II|qid=Q362|lt=Second World War}} and subsequent carrier shortages, many taiko platforms were abolished.  
At its peak in the old city district, there were roughly 30 district groups’ worth of futon taiko—comparable to the total number currently in Sakai City.

*(In some renditions the line “Thus it is the Hassaku rain” is omitted.)*
*Verse 3*  
*(Once sung mainly in the old city district; now preserved only at select sites such as Kaishenhama.)*
In addition, many districts have their own original festival songs.
【Victory Shout】  
"Yāe, Yāe, Āyoiyamakasokojaina, Yōiyase!"

== Abolished Futon Taiko ==
Due to air raids during the {{ill|World War II|en|World War II|qid=Q362|lt=Second World War}} and subsequent carrier shortages, many taiko platforms were abolished.  
At its peak in the old city district, there were roughly 30 district groups’ worth of futon taiko—comparable to the total number currently in Sakai City.
